newsitem.title: KENYA: Zaire rebels target Shaba, Mbuji-Mayi before truce.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels target Shaba, Mbuji-Mayi before truce.

text.p: Zairean rebels are unlikely to agree to a ceasefire until they have irreversibly broken the back of the government of President Mobutu Sese Seko, a regional military source said on Monday.
The devastating blow would be dealt by the rebels capturing the mineral-rich Shaba region and the diamond centre of Mbuji-Mayi, he said.

The source, who closely monitors the war between Laurent Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL) and Zaire's ragged and fast retreating mercenary-backed army, said the ADFL was consolidating troops in Shaba province.

He said the troop consolidation in the volatile region, where the embattled Kinshasa government has deployed the elite presidential guard, was in preparation for a final assault on the Shaba capital Lubumbashi.
"All our information and intelligence points to the fact that they (rebels) are unlikely to agree to a ceasefire before taking Lubumbashi," the source said.

"They are also eyeing Mbuji-Mayi and troop movements in that direction have been detected. The central political theme in the Alliance is they need Lubumbashi and Mbuji-Mayi to irreversibly break Mobutu," he said.
"Once the two areas are taken, the rebels believe it will be impossible for Mobutu to survive or to be intransigent at the negotiating table. He will have no economy to talk of."

The source said rebel forces were advancing towards the town of Kasenga 190 km (120 miles) from Lubumbashi. Other frontline fighting units were moving from Kabila's home village of Manono towards the huge American-built military base at Kamina some 310 km (190 miles) away.

The political climate in rebellion-prone Shaba will make it extremely difficult for the Zairean army and even the well-equipped and better paid presidential guard to mount a good fight against the rebels, the source added.
Reporters in Lubumbashi say the people of Shaba province, whose mineral wealth has helped keep Mobutu's Zaire afloat during three decades of ruinous rule, have high hopes of Kabila's rebellion.
Ordinary Shaba people complain that corruption and self-enrichment by officials have eaten away at hopes of economic progress.
Shaba region, better known locally by its traditional name Katanga, is sitting on some of the world's richest reserves of copper, cobalt and other precious minerals.
Opposition to Mobutu's government runs high in Shaba province in the south which has fought several times in vain for secession during Mobutu's 32 years in power in Zaire.
Alliance officials say their forces are moving fast towards the diamond capital Mbuji-Mayi and frontline units were within 100 km (60 miles) reach of the city, a view backed by the regional source.
The alliance already controls more than a fifth of the giant but chaotic Central African nation.
The source said Kabila had come under intense international pressure to agree to a ceasefire and South Africa had dispatched an envoy on Monday to sound him out on latest proposals.
"The South Africans have sent people to see Kabila in Kisangani. They are on their way there as we talk," the source added.
Kabila has refused to attend a special summit on Wednesday of the Organisation of African Unity (OAU) called to tackle the Zaire crisis but he dispatched a senior aide to represent him.
And in a major drawback for the summit, officials in Rwanda and Uganda said the two countries -- accused by Zaire of backing Kabila's forces -- would only send low-level ministerial delegations.
Rwanda is sending Foreign Minister Anastaza Gasana while Uganda will be represented by Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and Regional Cooperation Rebecca Kadaga.

Analysts said without the personal attendance of Ugandan president and regional power broker Yoweri Museveni and Rwandan President Pasteur Bizimungu, it will be impossible for the OAU summit to extract a truce out of the victorious rebels.
